This is what is called a review. They are very common and very useful. The way that science works is that many researchers conduct different experiments on different populations and draw conclusions from those experiments. Single experiments do not lend themselves to broad conclusions; hypotheses have little quirks and fringe cases that oven necessitate many experiments---tweaks and replications. Reviews aggregate these experiments and discuss the commonalities between their methods and findings and discuss trends over time. Another more restricted (but more powerful) aggregation approach is called meta-analysis.

If I'm not mistaken the US law covers two cases for this, which works pretty well for me:

  1. Civil cases: need a preponderance of evidence, which I translate to 70-80% or more.
  2. Criminal cases: need a conviction beyond reasonable doubt which I would put somewhere between 90-100%.

This distinction is made because in criminal cases if a judge or jury is wrong they could on extreme cases jail an innocent for life or even give him the death penalty so you absolutely don't want to claim someone is a criminal unless you're very positive about it being true.
